facts.text: DePauw began in 1837 as Indiana Asbury University, founded by the Methodist Church and named for Francis Asbury, the first American bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church.
DePauw admitted a small group of women in 1867.
Kappa Alpha Theta was founded at DePauw (then Indiana Asbury) on Jan 27, 1870. DePauw calls it the first sorority in the nation, and Alpha Chi Omega’s Alpha chapter began there too.
The Rector Scholarship, begun in 1919, is DePauw’s oldest merit academic award.
DePauw’s nature park covers 520 acres, one-third of a mile west of campus.
Indiana’s first Phi Beta Kappa chapter is at DePauw.
DePauw’s radio station, WGRE, was the first collegiate FM station in the country, on the air in 1949.
A massive granite boulder, given to DePauw in 1892, sits in front of East College.
Every January, DePauw students take part in Winter Term, a four-week immersive experience.
The Society of Professional Journalists was founded on DePauw’s campus in 1909.
Indiana Asbury University became DePauw University in appreciation of gifts from Washington C. DePauw and his family.
East College and McKim Observatory, built in 1884, are both listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
The Janet Prindle Institute for Ethics, funded by a gift from Janet Prindle ’58, sits in the DePauw Nature Park. Its building opened in 2007.
DePauw’s music school was established in 1884 with a gift from Washington C. DePauw and is one of the oldest in the country.
D3TV, DePauw’s internet-distributed campus television station, was established in 1995.
DePauw’s teams became the Tigers in 1917–18, when a campus contest picked the name over Yellowjackets, Wasps, and Yellow Demons. The colors are old gold and black.
Greencastle residents raised $25,000, then a huge sum, to bring the new university to town. Indiana’s General Assembly chartered it on Jan 10, 1837.
Indiana Asbury opened with one professor and five students. Its first class graduated three years later.
Matthew Simpson, Indiana Asbury’s first president, was a friend and counselor of Abraham Lincoln.
East College, whose cornerstone was laid in 1870, was first called “The Edifice.” It once held classrooms, the chapel, the library, and for a short time a telescope in its east tower.
Meharry Hall, the chapel on East College’s second floor, was designed to be “one of the most elegant audience rooms in the West.”
Before it came to DePauw, the Boulder sat on Hiram Thomas’s farm, where he charged visitors 10 cents to see what he called a petrified turtle.

facts.text: Alumni bought the Boulder and brought it to campus by the Monon Railroad and a wagon drawn by 26 horses.
The first Boulder, placed by the senior class in 1877, weighed 5,000 pounds and bore the class motto in Greek, “Andrizometha,” or “Let us be manly.”

sources.label: DePauw archives: Symbols of old DePauw

facts.text: DePauw’s Little 5 bike race began in 1956, when the Union Board held a men’s race to raise money for the American Cancer Society.
The DePauw, the student newspaper, began in 1852 as Asbury Notes. It is Indiana’s oldest college newspaper.
Old Gold Day began in 1907 to end increasingly violent freshman-sophomore class scraps. By 1919 it had grown into a full homecoming weekend.
The Arch at the end of Anderson Street, with “DPU” at its peak, was the class of 1890’s gift at its 20th reunion in 1910.

sources.label: DePauw archives: Symbols of old DePauw

facts.text: An early DePauw college yell was first given at the DePauw-Butler football game in Indianapolis on Nov 1, 1890.
DePauw classes began putting their numerals on the standpipe in Feb 1889. One member of the class of 1892 used orange letters seven feet long.
In the early 1880s, sophomores began wearing plug hats, starting a custom of each class choosing its own garb. The juniors soon took the “Oxford hat.”
Caps and gowns did not arrive at DePauw until 1894, when seniors first wore them. Tradition says juniors tried to confiscate them on their first appearance.
In World War I, 500 men were inducted into DePauw’s Students’ Army Training Corps on Oct 1, 1918, in a ceremony near the Boulder.
DePauw rules once forbade couples from riding to Halfway House, a dinner spot known for its cherry preserves, in a “single rig,” or two-seated buggy.
Cliffs of Fern, an old DePauw student haunt, was once so popular that the railroad ran excursion trains to it from Terre Haute and Indianapolis.
Percy Julian, DePauw’s 1920 valedictorian, later returned to research in its Minshall Laboratory and synthesized physostigmine, a drug used to treat glaucoma.
Wabash was founded on Nov 21, 1832, and its founders knelt in the snow the next day to dedicate the school.
Wabash has always been independent and non-sectarian.
Wabash’s history says Caleb Mills, an early figure at the college, later became the father of the Indiana public school system.
Each fall, Wabash uses Caleb Mills’ bell to ring in the freshman class, and each spring it rings out the graduating class.
Student conduct at Wabash is governed by the Gentleman’s Rule: behave as a gentleman and a responsible citizen.
Wabash got the nickname Little Giants in 1904, from an Indianapolis News sportswriter talking with coach Francis Cayou.
The phrase “Wabash Always Fights” first appeared at a 1919 meeting of the Montgomery County Alumni Association.
“Old Wabash” was written in 1899, and Wabash calls it the nation’s longest fight song.
Scarlet became Wabash’s official school color in 1886.
Wabash’s mission is to educate men to think critically, act responsibly, lead effectively, and live humanely.
Wabash’s Malcolm X Institute of Black Studies was founded in 1970, according to the institute’s own page.

sources.label: Wabash: Malcolm X Institute of Black Studies

facts.text: Wabash’s college archives, part of Lilly Library, hold a Biblia Sacra printed in 1540 as their oldest volume.
At Chapel Sing, a Wabash tradition, freshmen show they know the words to “Old Wabash” and the alma mater.
The Wabash Democracy and Public Discourse initiative works to advance deliberation, discussion, debate, and advocacy.
Scarlet Yarns is a Wabash project in which alumni record their stories at the Big Bash reunion, modeled on StoryCorps.
The Sphinx Club, a Wabash student group dating to 1921, was founded purely for social purposes.
Wabash was born at a meeting in the home of James Thomson, considered the motivating force behind a college in what was then called the Wabash Country.
Wabash’s founders planned to begin as “a classical and English high school, rising into a college as soon as the wants of the country demand.”
On Dec 3, 1833, Caleb Mills met Wabash’s first class of twelve students in Forest Hall. For the next five years, that building was the college.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: Forest Hall, built in 1833, was bought by Caleb Mills in 1850 and later moved to the present campus. It was moved again in 1951 and reached its current spot in 1965.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: South Hall, Wabash’s first brick building, burned in 1838, soon after it opened. Crawfordsville’s citizens gave $5,000 to rebuild it in time for the fall 1839 term.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: Center Hall, begun in 1856 and built in three stages, is Wabash’s oldest surviving brick building.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: The 811-pound college bell in Center Hall was hung on Nov 8, 1876, at 29 cents a pound. Tugging its rope gives a sense of its heft.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: Wabash’s Senior Bench is formally the Thomson Memorial Seat. Student groups paint it so often that its inscriptions are hard to read.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: Gen. Lew Wallace and poet James Whitcomb Riley took part in dedicating the Civil War tablet on Wabash’s Center Hall on June 17, 1902.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: More Wabash students fought and died at the Battle of Chickamauga than in any other Civil War battle.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: Hovey Rock, dedicated by the Class of 1876, honors founder Edmund Otis Hovey, generally considered the most important person in Wabash’s history.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: Pioneer Chapel was dedicated to the memory of Indiana pioneers on Jan 10, 1929. Before it, Wabash’s main buildings faced east, toward today’s Arboretum.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: Wabash’s Fuller Arboretum holds examples of most tree species native to Indiana.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: Wabash’s yell, “Wah-hoo-Wah! Wah-hoo-Wah! Wah-hoo! Wah-hoo! Wabash!”, lasted from 1886 until 1932, when it was modernized to “Hoo-Wah-Wah!”
The 1956 U.S. Olympic decathlon trials were held at Wabash, where Rafer Johnson, Milt Campbell, and Bob Richards competed before a capacity crowd at Ingalls Field.

sources.label: Wabash: When Wabash took center stage

facts.text: Wabash won the 1982 NCAA Division III men’s basketball championship, beating Potsdam State 83–62.
Before he went to Notre Dame and coached Knute Rockne, Jesse Harper was Wabash’s football coach.
The Wabash Little Giant Club was formed at Homecoming 1920 to honor every letterman since 1866, plus managers, cheerleaders, and champion orators.
Caleb Mills built his house in 1836. His descendants gave it to Wabash in 1926, and it became the home of Presidents Hopkins, Sparks, and Trippet.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: Since 1966, the Elston Homestead has been the official residence of Wabash’s presidents.

sources.label: Wabash: Buildings and important landmarks (campus tour)

facts.text: The Monon Bell is a locomotive bell from the Monon Railroad, and it became the rivalry’s trophy in 1932.
The Monon Bell weighs about 300 pounds, though reports have put it anywhere from 200 to 400.
The Monon Railroad line between Crawfordsville and Greencastle often carried the teams to the game.
If the Monon Bell game ends in a tie, the team that held the Bell going in keeps it.
“The Ballad of the Monon Bell,” a song about the rivalry, was recorded in 1985.
DePauw and Wabash are both members of the Great Lakes Colleges Association.

sources.label: Great Lakes Colleges Association: Our colleges

facts.text: DePauw and Wabash both compete in the North Coast Athletic Conference, which DePauw joined effective July 1, 2011.
